groups.label: Civic Duties of Medicine and Law
groups.summary: Socrates contrasts the roles of physicians and judges, rejecting valetudinarian practices that prolong unproductive lives in favor of civic usefulness. He notes that while bodily doctors benefit from personal experience of illness, judges must acquire knowledge of vice late without personal corruption.
groups.rationale: Both passages from Book III examine civic professions (physicians and judges) and the proper limits of caring for body versus soul.

groups.label: Epistemology of Being and Opinion
groups.summary: Socrates defines the true philosopher as desiring the whole of wisdom and distinguishes between immutable singular Forms and the ambiguous, fluctuating particulars that embody opposing traits. He assigns knowledge to true being, ignorance to non-being, and opinion to the intermediate domain of sensory particulars.
groups.rationale: These adjacent Book V occurrences systematically define philosophy, Forms, intermediate faculties, and the fluctuating nature of particulars.

groups.label: Philosophers and Civic Hostility
groups.summary: Adeimantus raises the charge that philosophers are useless rogues, which Socrates answers with the parable of the mutinous ship mistreating its true navigator. Socrates explains that philosophy has been usurped by unworthy pretenders while the genuine remnant must shelter under a wall away from political corruption.
groups.rationale: These Book VI passages directly address the perceived uselessness of philosophers in flawed political regimes and describe the isolation of true thinkers.

groups.label: Reforming Dialectic and Publics
groups.summary: Socrates advocates reforming the sequence of philosophical education so that intensive dialectical study is deferred until maturity rather than pursued prematurely. He further argues that the multitude will overcome their animosity toward philosophy when shown true thinkers focused on divine order.
groups.rationale: Both passages treat remedies to the poor public standing of philosophy: restructuring its lifelong curriculum and reconciling with the general public.

groups.label: Enlightenment and Curriculum
groups.summary: The discussion transitions from accepting the divided schema of mental faculties into the Cave allegory, depicting prisoners chained before shadows who must undergo a dazzling ascent toward the sun. Socrates subsequently outlines the mathematical curriculum needed for this upward turn, emphasizing that solid geometry must precede astronomy.
groups.rationale: These entries cover the cognitive framework of enlightenment and the educational stages leading out of the cave in Books VI and VII.

groups.label: Pleasures of Smell Example
groups.summary: The sensation of scent is provided as an instance of pure pleasure that arises without prior suffering or deficit and departs without pain.
groups.rationale: This Book IX singleton treats the taxonomy of pleasure, remaining distinct in source location and topic from earlier dialectical and educational themes.

groups.label: Cosmic Spindle of Necessity
groups.summary: Souls witness the cosmic structure turned by the spindle of Necessity, governed by eight rotating concentric whorls, the sirens' harmonies, and the three Fates who guide past, present, and future.
groups.rationale: This Book X mythic vision of cosmic astronomy and eschatology is geographically and thematically isolated at the end of the dialogue.
